title: The history of the reproductive system
tagline: From a beating spot in a hen's egg to IVF babies in Oldham and Kolkata: how people learned where life begins.
intro: For most of history people could only guess how a new life starts. Microscopes in the 1600s revealed sperm and follicles, and in the 1800s scientists finally found the mammal egg and watched one sperm fertilise it. The 1900s brought chromosomes, hormones, ultrasound and IVF, and public health turned that knowledge into safer births, including in India, where far fewer mothers now die in childbirth.

eras.name: Big ideas, few tools
eras.summary: Thinkers open hens' eggs, name the tubes and argue that every animal comes from an egg, without being able to see one.

eras.name: Under the microscope
eras.summary: Microscopes reveal follicles and sperm, a wrong idea about tiny people is overturned, and the mammal egg is finally found.

eras.name: Cells, chromosomes and hormones
eras.summary: Scientists watch fertilisation happen, count chromosomes, find the X and Y, and discover the hormones that run the cycle and puberty.

eras.name: Safer births
eras.summary: Handwashing, trained doctors, ultrasound and photographs make pregnancy and birth safer and better understood.

eras.name: Help to have a baby
eras.summary: IVF babies are born in England and India within months of each other, and new methods help more couples.

eras.name: India's mothers and daughters
eras.summary: Laws protect girls, schemes bring births into hospitals, and maternal deaths fall by more than three-quarters.

events.title: Watching a chick grow inside an egg
events.text: Aristotle opened hens' eggs day after day and wrote down what he saw. By about the third day a tiny red spot appeared that beat like a heart. He argued that the body's parts form one after another, not all at once.
events.why: It was the first careful, step-by-step record of how an embryo develops.

events.title: The tubes get their name
events.text: The Italian anatomist Gabriele Falloppio described the two slender tubes that run from the uterus towards the ovaries, with their fringed, trumpet-like ends. His book Observationes Anatomicae was printed in Venice in 1561.
events.why: We still call them fallopian tubes, although nobody then knew that eggs travel along them.

events.title: "Everything from an egg"
events.text: William Harvey, famous for showing how blood circulates, studied chicks and deer embryos. In his book On the Generation of Animals he argued that all animals, including humans, begin from some kind of egg. The phrase ex ovo omnia, everything from an egg, became linked to his work.
events.why: It pointed scientists towards the egg long before anyone had seen a mammal's egg.

events.title: Bubbles in the ovary
events.text: The Dutch doctor Regnier de Graaf studied the ovaries of rabbits and other mammals and described small fluid-filled bubbles on their surface. He thought each bubble was an egg. In fact each one holds a far smaller egg inside. We still call a ripe one a Graafian follicle.
events.why: He found the follicle, the bubble that ripens and releases an egg every month.

events.title: Sperm seen for the first time
events.text: Using his own tiny, powerful single-lens microscopes, the cloth merchant Antonie van Leeuwenhoek saw thousands of swimming cells with long tails in a sample of semen. A medical student, Johan Ham, had first pointed them out to him. He described them in a letter to the Royal Society in London.
events.why: For the first time, people could see the cell that carries the father's half of a new life.

events.title: A tiny person in the sperm?
events.text: The Dutch microscope maker Nicolaas Hartsoeker drew a tiny curled-up person, a homunculus, inside the head of a sperm. He did not claim to have seen it; he drew it to show an idea many people then held, that a miniature person was already formed and only had to grow.
events.why: It is a famous example of a wrong idea that microscopes and careful experiments later overturned.

events.title: Bodies build themselves step by step
events.text: In his thesis Theoria Generationis, the German scientist Caspar Friedrich Wolff showed from chick embryos that organs such as the gut form from simple, unshaped layers. Nothing was ready-made: the body builds itself in stages, an idea called epigenesis.
events.why: It replaced the tiny-person idea with the picture of development that biology still uses.

events.title: Proof that sperm are needed
events.text: The Italian priest and scientist Lazzaro Spallanzani showed that frog eggs only develop after they touch sperm-containing fluid. When he filtered the sperm out, the fluid no longer worked. He also carried out the first successful artificial insemination, in a dog.
events.why: Experiments, not just looking, showed that both the egg and the sperm are needed.

events.title: The mammal egg is found
events.text: Karl Ernst von Baer opened a follicle from a dog's ovary and found a tiny yellowish speck floating inside it. It was the real egg, far smaller than de Graaf's bubble. He published the discovery in a short Latin book.
events.why: It settled a 150-year-old question: mammals, including humans, do begin from a single egg cell.

events.title: Clean hands save mothers
events.text: Ignaz Semmelweis noticed that far more mothers died of childbed fever on the ward run by doctors, who came straight from dissections, than on the ward run by midwives. He made staff wash their hands in chlorinated lime, and deaths on his ward dropped sharply.
events.why: Handwashing became one of the simplest and most powerful ways to keep mothers and babies safe.

events.title: Watching one sperm enter an egg
events.where: Mediterranean coast (sea urchin eggs); based at Jena, Germany
events.text: Oscar Hertwig studied the clear eggs of a Mediterranean sea urchin, which are easy to see through. He mixed eggs and sperm and watched a single sperm enter an egg. About ten minutes later the sperm's nucleus had travelled to meet the egg's nucleus and joined with it.
events.why: It showed that fertilisation is the joining of one sperm and one egg, nucleus with nucleus.

events.title: Half the chromosomes from each parent
events.text: Working with the eggs of a roundworm that has very few chromosomes, Edouard van Beneden showed that the egg and the sperm each bring the same number of chromosomes, half of what the body's cells carry, and that they come together at fertilisation.
events.why: This is the idea behind 23 + 23 = 46 in humans.

events.title: India's first woman doctor of Western medicine
events.text: Anandibai Joshi lost her baby son days after birth, and resolved to study medicine. She sailed to the United States and graduated from the Woman's Medical College of Pennsylvania with a thesis on obstetrics among Hindus.
events.why: She showed Indian women could become doctors, and she chose care for mothers and babies as her subject.

events.title: The X and Y chromosomes
events.text: Studying mealworm beetles, Nettie Stevens found that females had pairs of large chromosomes, while males had one large and one small one. She concluded that the sperm's chromosome decides whether the young is female or male. Edmund Wilson reached a similar conclusion the same year.
events.why: It explained why the sperm, carrying an X or a Y, sets a baby's sex.

events.title: The ovary's hormone
events.text: Edgar Allen and Edward Doisy extracted a substance from pig ovary follicles that made the lining of the uterus grow and brought animals into their breeding cycle. It was oestrogen. Doisy later purified it, and progesterone was found a few years afterwards.
events.why: It showed that the menstrual cycle is run by hormones from the ovary.

events.title: Humans have 46 chromosomes
events.who: Joe Hin Tjio and Albert Levan
events.text: For thirty years textbooks said humans had 48 chromosomes. Using better ways to spread cells out on a slide, Joe Hin Tjio counted 46 again and again, and he and Albert Levan published the result.
events.why: It fixed the number at the heart of this box: 23 from each parent, 46 in all.

events.title: Seeing the baby with sound
events.who: Ian Donald, John MacVicar and Tom Brown
events.text: A Glasgow obstetrician, Ian Donald, worked with a doctor and an engineer to adapt an ultrasound machine used for finding cracks in metal. Their paper in The Lancet showed pictures of the inside of the belly made with sound echoes. Soon ultrasound could show a growing baby safely, without X-rays.
events.why: Ultrasound scans became a routine, safe way to check a baby's growth.

events.title: Life before birth on a magazine cover
events.text: The Swedish photographer Lennart Nilsson spent years taking pictures of human embryos and fetuses with special cameras and lenses. Life magazine printed them as Drama of Life Before Birth, and millions of copies sold within days.
events.why: For many people it was the first time they saw how a baby develops.

events.title: The brain's 'start' hormone
events.who: Andrew Schally and Roger Guillemin (separate teams)
events.where: New Orleans and La Jolla, USA
events.text: Working with extracts from hundreds of thousands of pig and sheep brains, Andrew Schally's team worked out the structure of GnRH, the hypothalamus hormone that tells the pituitary to release LH and FSH. Roger Guillemin's team confirmed it. They shared the 1977 Nobel Prize with Rosalyn Yalow.
events.why: It explained how the brain switches on puberty and runs the menstrual cycle.

events.title: Louise Brown, the first IVF baby
events.who: Patrick Steptoe and Robert Edwards (with Jean Purdy)
events.text: After years of work, a gynaecologist and a scientist joined an egg and sperm in a lab dish and placed the early embryo in the mother's uterus. Louise Brown was born healthy. Robert Edwards received the Nobel Prize in 2010.
events.why: It gave hope to millions of people with infertility.

events.title: Durga, India's first IVF baby
events.who: Dr Subhas Mukhopadhyay (with Sunit Mukherji and Saroj Kanti Bhattacharya)
events.text: Just 70 days after Louise Brown, a baby girl named Durga, later known as Kanupriya Agarwal, was born in Kolkata. Dr Subhas Mukhopadhyay and his colleagues had used their own methods and simple equipment. A government committee refused to believe him, and he died in 1981. Years later, experts reviewed his notes and recognised his work.
events.why: India was only the second country with an IVF baby, and Mukhopadhyay is now honoured as a pioneer.

events.title: Harsha, India's first documented IVF baby
events.who: Dr Indira Hinduja, with T. C. Anand Kumar's ICMR team
events.text: A baby boy named Harsha was born at KEM Hospital in Mumbai after IVF by Dr Indira Hinduja and a team from the Indian Council of Medical Research's Institute for Research in Reproduction.
events.why: It started IVF as a medical service in India, which now has thousands of fertility clinics.

events.title: One sperm, injected
events.text: Doctors in Brussels reported the first pregnancies after injecting a single sperm directly into an egg with a very fine glass needle. The method is called ICSI.
events.why: It helped many couples where the male partner has very few sperm.

events.title: A law against sex selection
events.text: India passed the Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques Act, later renamed the PCPNDT Act. It bans using scans or tests to find out or choose the sex of a baby before birth.
events.why: It protects girls, because the sperm, not anyone's choice, decides a baby's sex.

events.title: Help to give birth safely
events.who: Janani Suraksha Yojana, National Rural Health Mission
events.text: The Government of India launched Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY), which gives cash help to poorer mothers who give birth in a hospital or health centre, supported by community health workers called ASHAs.
events.why: Births in health facilities rose steeply, to 88.6% by 2019–21.

events.title: A free check-up on the 9th of every month
events.text: The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare launched PMSMA, which offers every pregnant woman in her second or third trimester a free check-up by a doctor on the 9th day of every month at government health centres.
events.why: Regular check-ups catch problems like high blood pressure and anaemia before they become dangerous.

events.title: India's maternal deaths fall below 100
events.who: Sample Registration System, Registrar General of India
events.text: The Sample Registration System, which tracks births and deaths in a large national sample, reported a maternal mortality ratio of 88 deaths per 100,000 live births for 2020–22. In 1997–98 it had been 398.
events.why: It is a fall of more than three-quarters in about 25 years, though some states still have far higher rates.

series.caption: India's maternal mortality ratio from the Sample Registration System, plotted at the middle year of each period. It fell from 398 in 1997–98 to 88 in 2020–22.

facts: The human egg, about 0.1 mm across, is the largest cell in the body and only just visible without a microscope.
A girl is born with about 1 to 2 million immature eggs, but only about 400 to 500 are ever released.
For about 30 years, textbooks wrongly said humans have 48 chromosomes.
Durga, India's first IVF baby, was born just 70 days after Louise Brown, the world's first.
In 2019–21, 77% of young women in India used a hygienic method during their periods, up from 58% in 2015–16.
